claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is controlled by dislocation accumulation at the interfaces.
FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers exhibit high or severe lattice distortion.
FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers possess pronounced short-range order.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation transmission across the layers and their interfaces.
Short-range order impedes dislocation transmission across the layers and their interfaces.
Obstructed dislocation transmission causes dislocation pile-ups at FCC/BCC boundaries under sustained stress.
Interfacial dislocation pile-ups trigger localized interface sliding after reaching a critical density.
Localized interface sliding, rather than homogeneous bulk creep, produces the progressive plastic deformation.
The proposed interface-sliding deformation can occur while the nanolayer architecture remains intact.
The starting multilayers have clean nanoscale FCC/BCC interfaces and minimal initial dislocation content.
Under sustained loading, the creep rate should initially be low and then accelerate as interfacial dislocation pile-ups develop.
Sustained loading should increase dislocation density at FCC/BCC boundaries relative to the pristine baseline.
Sustained loading should produce localized interface-shear signatures such as offsets or ledges at FCC/BCC boundaries.
As-deposited multilayers with minimal interfacial dislocations exhibit a lower, steady creep rate under comparable loading and temperature conditions.
Changing layer thickness or interface chemistry may produce different deformation regimes.
An interface modification that prevents dislocation accumulation should delay or reduce the onset of plastic deformation.
